move: Attacks the a priori proof by arguing that we can always conceive the non-existence of anything we conceive to exist, so the phrase 'necessary existence' has no consistent meaning.

Runs a disjunctive proof that no cause annulling God's existence can be drawn either from his own nature or from another substance, and adds that finite beings cannot be more powerful in existing than an absolutely infinite being.
Argues a priori from potentiality of existence as power that a being of absolutely infinite reality has infinite power of existing from itself, and therefore absolutely exists.
Treats the existence of particular things as following from the eternal necessity of God's nature and concludes that the human mind's idea of God's eternal and infinite essence is adequate.
Argues that produced things' essences do not involve existence, so God, whose nature involves existence, is self-caused and the continuing cause of the being of all things.
Summarizes the preceding demonstrations as having shown that God necessarily exists, is one, and acts by the necessity of his own nature, then turns to clearing away prejudices against those proofs.

Sets the existence question aside to ask instead what kind of being God would be if he existed, insisting that 'God' must name something with definite intrinsic attributes before the debate can bear fruit.
Argues from the world's ills that, while the world may be consistent with a powerful, wise, benevolent Deity, it licenses no inference to his existence, so the proper attitude is scepticism.
Illustrates with rectangles contained in a circle how ideas of particular things exist within the infinite idea of God, expounding the doctrine rather than arguing for or against God's existence.
Invokes God's necessary rather than contingent existence as a premise for showing that all things are conditioned by the necessity of the divine nature and nothing is contingent.
Argues that existence appertains to the nature of substance, hence God is eternal and his existence and essence are one and the same eternal truth.
Clarifies a definitional point — individual things cannot be or be conceived without God, yet God does not belong to their essence — while working out what constitutes the human mind.
